summary: A reply to Wayne Hathaway's RFC 513 about the Telnet SYNCH sequence. The authors agree that the phrase interesting things is too vague for a specification, but disagree that SYNCH should be redefined. They argue the problems come from higher-level protocols such as FTP misusing it.

plainLanguage.summary: This note explains why a synchronization signal has both an attention signal and a marker in the data stream. It argues that each protocol layer should define its own synchronization rules.

questions: what is the telnet synch sequence
what is the telnet data mark
how to abort an ftp transfer over telnet
subtitle: An argument for defining separate synchronization sequences at different protocol levels.

tldr.problem: RFC 513 questions Telnet's SYNCH behavior, but RFC 529 argues the difficulty comes from higher-level protocols trying to use Telnet's mechanism for their own commands.
tldr.mechanism: The note explains SYNCH as an out-of-band signal plus an in-band marker, and recommends that protocols built on Telnet define their own marker and use Telnet IP to get attention.
tldr.outcome: The authors retain Telnet's SYNCH definition and argue that higher-level protocols should not assign it a second meaning.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 529 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. It responds to the Telnet SYNCH comments in RFC 513.

sections.title: What a SYNCH Sequence Does
sections.content:
The authors respond to RFC 513. They agree that the phrase interesting things is too vague for a protocol specification, but they do not agree that Telnet's SYNCH definition should be changed.

A SYNCH sequence has an out-of-band signal that gets the interpreter's attention and an in-band marker that shows how much of the stream to process.
sections.plainLanguage: A synchronization sequence first gets the receiver's attention, then marks where scanning should stop. Telnet uses INS for attention and Data Mark as the marker.

sections.title: Keeping Protocol Layers Separate
sections.content:
For Telnet, the note identifies Host-Host INS as the out-of-band signal and Telnet Data Mark as the in-band marker. Telnet commands are the items its interpreter must recognize; a host may also pass other local terminal signals to its process.

The authors say a Telnet interpreter cannot know which data is important to every higher-level protocol. Using Telnet SYNCH to carry higher-level commands gives the same mechanism meaning at two levels.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet should interpret Telnet commands, while a higher-level protocol should interpret its own commands. The lower layer should not need to understand every service above it.

sections.title: A Higher-Level SYNCH
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that a higher-level protocol define its own synchronization sequence when it needs to bring commands through to its interpreter. The proposed pattern inserts Telnet IP to interrupt processing, then places a higher-level data mark after the commands that matter.

For the FTP abort example, the user sends Telnet IP, the Telnet SYNCH sequence, the FTP ABOR command, and then the FTP data mark. The note says the FTP data mark had not yet been defined.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol above Telnet can use Telnet IP to get attention, then its own marker to end the scan. This keeps the two protocols' rules separate.
